SUPLEMENTAÇÃO DE CURCUMINA E ALTERAÇÕES AO LONGO
DO TEMPO EM MARCADORES DE ESTRESSE METABÓLICO,
INFLAMATÓRIO E OXIDATIVO EM PESSOAS VIVENDO COM HIV
E DISLIPIDEMIA: UM ENSAIO CLÍNICO RANDOMIZADO, DUPLO-
CEGO E CRUZADO

Resumo
Pessoas vivendo com HIV (PVHIV) apresentam ativação imune persistente,
estresse oxidativo e alta prevalência de distúrbios metabólicos, incluindo
dislipidemia, que aumentam o risco cardiovascular. A curcumina, um composto
polifenólico derivado da Curcuma l onga, exibe propriedades antioxidantes e anti -
inflamatórias e pode representar uma estratégia adjuvante para a modulação redox
e metabólica. Este estudo avaliou os efeitos da suplementação com curcumina
sobre marcadores metabólicos, inflamatórios e de estr esse oxidativo em PVHIV
com dislipidemia. Um ensaio clínico cruzado, randomizado, duplo -cego e
controlado por placebo foi conduzido em um serviço especializado em atendimento
a pessoas vivendo com HIV no sul do Brasil. Adultos em terapia antirretroviral
estável por pelo menos seis meses e com diagnóstico de dislipidemia receberam
curcumina (1000 mg/dia) ou placebo durante dois períodos de intervenção
separados por uma fase de washout. Os desfechos bioquímicos incluíram perfil
lipídico, enzimas hepáticas, gl icose, citocinas inflamatórias (IL -6, IL-10, TNF-α) e
marcadores de estresse oxidativo [substâncias reativas ao ácido tiobarbitúrico
(TBARS) e capacidade antioxidante total (CAT)]. Os dados foram analisados por
meio de ANOVA de medidas repetidas, avalian do grupo, tempo e interação grupo
× tempo. Dezesseis participantes foram incluídos (idade média de 44,7 ± 1,2 anos;
68,8% do sexo feminino ), com adesão adequada. Uma interação grupo × tempo
significativa foi observada apenas para o colesterol total (p = 0,034). Efeitos
significativos do tempo foram identificados para o colesterol HDL (p = 0,004),
triglicerídeos (p = 0,003), AST (p = 0,021), hemoglobina glicada (p = 0,014), TBARS
plasmático (p = 0,049) e CAT (p = 0,003). Observou -se redução nos níveis de
triglicerídeos e TBARS, além de aumento na capacidade antioxidante, ao longo do
período de acompanhamento, independentemente da sequência de intervenção.
As citocinas inflamatórias apresentaram marcada variabilidade interindividual. A

suplementação com curcumina associou-se a alterações longitudinais no estresse
oxidativo e em marcadores metabólicos, embora os efeitos específicos do
tratamento em comparação com o placebo tenham sido limitados. Ensaios clínicos
de maior porte, com desfechos oxidativos predefinidos, são necessários para
confirmar esses achados.

CURCUMIN SUPPLEMENTATION AND CHANGES OVER TIME IN METABOLIC,
INFLAMMATORY, AND OXIDATIVE STRESS MARKERS IN PEOPLE LIVING WITH HIV
AND DYSLIPIDEMIA: A RANDOMIZED DOUBLE-BLIND CROSSOVER TRIAL

Abstract
People living with HIV (PLHIV) present persi stent immune activation, oxidative
stress, and a high prevalence of metabolic disturbances, including dyslipidemia,
which increase cardiovascular risk. Curcumin, a polyphenolic compound derived
from Curcuma longa, exhibits antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties and may
represent an adjuvant strategy for redox and metabolic modulation. This study
evaluated the effects of curcumin supplementation on metabolic, inflammatory, and
oxidative stress markers in PLHIV with dyslipidemia. A randomized, double -blind,
placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial was conducted at a specialized HIV care
service in southern Brazil. Adults receiving stable antiretroviral therapy for at least
six months and diagnosed with dyslipidemia received curcumin (1000 mg/day) or
placebo during two intervention periods separated by a washout phase. Biochemical
outcomes included lipid profile, liver enzymes, glucose, inflammatory cytokines (IL-
6, IL -10, TNF -α), and oxidative stress markers [thiobarbituric acid reactive
substances (TB ARS) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC)]. Data were analyzed
using repeated -measures ANOVA assessing group, time, and group × time
interaction. Sixteen participants were included (mean age 44.7 ± 1.2 years; 68.8%
female), with adequate adherence. A significant group × time interaction was
observed only for total cholesterol (p = 0.034). Significant time effects were identified
for HDL-cholesterol (p = 0.004), triglycerides (p = 0.003), AST (p = 0.021), glycated
hemoglobin (p = 0.014), plasma TBARS (p = 0.049), and TAC (p = 0.003).
Reductions in triglycerides and TBARS and increased antioxidant capacity were
observed throughout the follow -up, regardless of intervention sequence.
Inflammatory cytokines showed marked interindividual variability. Curcumin
supplementation was associated with longitudinal changes in oxidative stress and
metabolic markers, although treatment-specific effects versus placebo were limited.
Larger trials with predefined oxidative endpoints are needed to confirm these
findings.

Keywords: AIDS; Curcuma longa , Oxidative stress, Dyslipidemia, Inflammatory
markers

1. Introduction
Chronic HIV infection, even under sustained viral suppression with antiretroviral
therapy (ART), is characterized by persistent immune activation and systemic
oxidative stress. Viral proteins such as Tat, Nef, and gp120 contribute to increased
production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) through activation of NADPH oxidases
and mitochondrial dysfunction, while residual microbial translocation maintains
inflammatory signaling pathways, including NF -κB activation [1–4]. As a
consequence, people living with HIV (PLHIV) exhibit a persistent imbalance
between oxidant production and antioxidant defense mechanisms, even in the
absence of detectable viremia [4,5].
Dysregulation of redox homeostasis in treated HIV infection has been associated
with lipid peroxidation, endothelial dysfunction, metabolic alterations, and features
of accelerated aging [6,7]. Reduced glutathione availability, impaired activity of
antioxidant enzymes, and alterations in the Nrf2 –Keap1 pathway have been
described in this population, reinforcing the concept of HIV as a clinical model of
chronic immune activati on and sustained oxidative stress [5,8]. Although
antiretroviral therapy (ART) effectively controls viral replication, it does not fully
restore redox balance and may even contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction and
persistent oxidative damage [3,9]. This sustained pro -oxidant state is closely
associated with metabolic comorbidities frequently observed in people living with
HIV (PLHIV), including dyslipidemia and components of the metabolic syndrome
[7,10].
Curcumin, the main polyphenolic constituent of Curcuma longa L., has been
widely investigated for its pleiotropic biological properties. In addition to its direct
free-radical scavenging capacity, curcumin modulates key intracellular signaling
cascades, including inhibition of NF -κB activation, activation of the Nrf2 pathway,
regulation of mitochondrial function, and epigenetic modulation of inflammatory
gene expression [11,12]. Experimental studies demonstrate that curcumin
enhances endogenous antioxidant defenses through induction of heme oxygenase-
1 (HO-1) via Nrf2 activation and reduces lipid peroxidation and cytokine production
in inflammatory and metabolic models [13–15]. These findings suggest that

14

curcumin acts as a regulator of systemic redox homeostasis rather t han merely as
a conventional antioxidant.
Despite robust preclinical evidence supporting the redox -modulating properties
of curcumin, controlled clinical studies evaluating its mechanistic effects under
conditions characterized by persistent immune activation remain limited. In
particular, the pot ential of curcumin to modulate oxidative stress biomarkers in
treated HIV infection—a clinical context marked by chronic inflammatory signaling
and metabolic dysregulation—remains insufficiently explored [8,16].
Accordingly, the present randomized, double -blind, placebo -controlled
crossover clinical trial was designed to evaluate the effects of curcumin
supplementation on lipid profile (primary outcome) and, secondarily, to investigate
its influence on systemic biomarkers of oxidative stress and inflammation in people
living with HIV and dyslipidemia receiving stable antiretroviral therapy (ART), using
this population as a clinical model of chronic immune activation and redox
imbalance.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Study design
This study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical
trial conducted in accordance with the CONSORT guidelines and the principles of
the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics
Committee of the State University of Western Paraná (protocol no. 7,049,856). All
participants provided written i nformed consent prior to inclusion. The trial was
registered in the Brazilian Clinical Trials Registry (ReBEC; RBR-7y5p3x8).

2.2 Study setting and participants
Participants were recruited from the Specialized Care Service (SAE/CTA) in
the municipality of Francisco Beltrão, Paraná, Brazil. Eligible individuals were adults
aged 35 to 50 years living with HIV, receiving stable antiretroviral therapy (ART) for
at least six months, and diagnosed with dyslipidemia according to the Brazilian
Guidelines for Dyslipidemia and Atherosclerosis Prevention [17]. Dyslipidemia was
defined as the presence of at least one abnormal lipid parameter: total cholesterol
≥190 mg/dL, HDL-cholesterol <40 mg/dL, or triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL.

15

Pregnant women and in dividuals unable to ingest capsules were excluded.
Participants were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time
without any impact on their routine clinical care.

2.3 Randomization and blinding
Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to one of two intervention
sequences: curcumin followed by placebo or placebo followed by curcumin. The
randomization s equence was computer -generated in blocks by an independent
pharmacist who was not involved in data collection or statistical analysis. Allocation
concealment was ensured through the use of coded bottles. Participants,
researchers, laboratory staff, and sta tisticians remained blinded to treatment
allocation throughout the study. The assessments were carried out at four time
points (T1–T4), as shown in the table.

2.4 Intervention
The intervention consisted of the administration of 1000 mg/day of Curcuma
longa L. (rhizome) dry extract, standardized to 95% curcuminoids, provided as two
500 mg capsules. The botanical material was taxonomically identified by a qualified
botanist, and a voucher specimen was deposited in the Herbarium of Itaipu
Binacional under registration number 05.06/24. The plant material consisted of dried
rhizomes of Curcuma longa L.
The botanical material was obtained from certified suppliers and
manufactured according to Good Compounding Practices, in accordance with
ANVISA RDC No. 67/2007. T he extract (CUR240401) was standardized to 95%
curcuminoids, as determined in the analytical report validated by the manufacturer.
Each intervention period lasted 12 weeks and was separated by a 4 -week
washout period, based on pharmacokinetic consideratio ns related to curcumin
metabolism and elimination [18].
The placebo contained the same excipients, with the addition of food coloring,
ensuring similar sensory characteristics.

17

2.5 Sample size
The sample size calculation was performed using G*Power software,
considering α = 0.05, statistical power of 80%, and an effect size of 0.25, resulting
in a minimum estimated sample of 34 participants. Due to recruitment limitations,
the final sample consi sted of 16 participants, and this limitation was taken into
account in the interpretation of the results.

2.6 Laboratory analyses
Blood samples were collected after a minimum fasting period of 12 hours.
Routine biochemical analyses (total cholesterol, triglycerides, AST, ALT, and
fasting glucose) were performed using commercial kits (Ebram) in a semi-automatic
spectrophotometer (BT 3000 Plus). Glycated hemoglobin was determined using
Analisa® kits. Inflammatory cytokines (IL -6, IL-10, and TNF -α) were qu antified by
ELISA (Thermo Fisher Scientific), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Oxidative stress biomarkers were analyzed at the Laboratory of Human and Animal
BioHealth (Federal University of Fronteira Sul). Intracellular ROS production was
assessed using the DCHF -DA assay, as described by Loetchutinat et al. [19].
Fluorescence was measured with excitation at 488 nm and emission at 520 nm, and
results were expressed in arbitrary units (AU). TBARS, total antioxidant capacity
(TAC), total thiols, and vitamin C were determined using standardized
spectrophotometric methods.

2.7 Outcomes and Statistical Analysis
The primary outcome was the change in lipid profile (total cholesterol, HDL -
c, LDL -c, and triglycerides). Secondary outcomes included oxidative stress
biomarkers (TBARS, TAC, total thiols, vitamin C, and ROS), inflammatory cytokines
(IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α), and metabolic parameters (fasting glucose, HbA1c, AST,
and ALT).
For sample characterization, categorical variables were described as
absolute and relative frequencies, and continuous variables as mean and standard
deviation. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro –Wilk test,
homogeneity of variances by Levene’s test, and sphericity by Mauchly’s test. When

18

necessary, logarithmic transformations were performed to meet the assumptions of
parametric statistics.
Considering the crossover design, comparisons between groups over time
were conducted using repeated -measures Analysis of Variance (ANOVA),
evaluating group effects, time effects, and group × time interaction effects. Due to
the small sample size , formal tests to assess sequence or carryover effects were
not performed, and the results were interpreted with caution.
Additionally, intragroup analyses were conducted using the nonparametric
Friedman test, comparing the four assessment time points with in each sequence.
All analyses were performed using SPSS software, version 29.0, with a significance
level set at 5% (p < 0.05).

3. Results
The final sample consisted of 16 participants, with 9 allocated to the
curcumin–placebo sequence and 7 to the placebo –curcumin sequence. Table 1
presents the general characteristics of the sample, stratified by groups according to

mean age of 44.7 ± 1.2 years; 68.8% female . Proportionally, participants who
started with the placebo treatment reported a higher frequency of employment. Most
participants had completed high school, we re non -smokers, and reported no
cardiovascular disease or diabetes mellitus. Participants who started treatment with
curcumin showed a higher frequency of alcohol consumption and physical activity
practice. Among the participants, two were receiving simvas tatin as hypolipidemic
therapy for dyslipidemia control.

4. Discussion
In this randomized, double -blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial,
curcumin supplementation was associated with time -related changes in oxidative
stress markers and some metabolic parameters in people living with HIV (PLWH)
with dyslipidemia. Although lipid parameters were defined as the primary outcomes
in the study registration, the most consistent longitudinal signals were observed in
redox biomarkers, with a reduction in plasma TBARS and an increase in antioxidant
capacity over the follow -up period. This pattern suggests that curcumin may exert
earlier or more readily detectable effects on redox balance than on lipid metabolism
in this clinical context.
Oxidative stress is recognized as a central component of HIV -1 infection, being
present from the early stages of the disease, increasing as the disease progresses,
and persisting even in individuals receiving effective antiretroviral therapy. Evidence
indicates that HIV infection promotes redox imbalance through the dysregulation of
multiple cellular pathways, resulting in increased ROS production and mitochondrial
dysfunction [9]. This increase in ROS is mediated by several viral proteins, including
the envelope glycoprotein gp120, Tat, Nef, Vpr, and reverse transcriptase, which
act complementarily across different cell types. The activation of pro -oxidant
systems, such as NADPH oxidases, cytochrome P450 2E1, and enzymes involved
in polyamine metabolism, contributes to excessive ROS generation, affecting
immune cells, cells of the central nervous system, and endothelial cells, thereby
reinforcing the systemic nature of oxidative st ress associated with HIV -1 infection
[4].
Oxidative stress is markedly exacerbated in people living with HIV com pared
with healthy controls, progressively increasing as the disease advances, with higher

22

levels observed in symptomatic compared with asymptomatic individuals. Evidence
indicates that although antiretroviral therapy (ART) is effective in suppressing vira l
replication, it is not sufficient to fully normalize redox balance and may even
contribute to the maintenance of oxidative stress through mitochondrial alterations,
residual inflammation, and metabolic effects associated with chronic antiretroviral
use [5]. This scenario favors the persistence of a pro -oxidant state associated with
metabolic disturbances, chronic inflammatory activation, immunosenescence, and
accelerated aging, even in individuals with undetectable viral load [3,20]
In this context, the findings of the present study gain biological rel evance. A
significant time effect was observed, with a reduction in plasma TBARS, a classical
marker of lipid peroxidation, and a progressive increase in total antioxidant capacity
assessed by the ferric reducing antioxidant power assay, regardless of trea tment
sequence. These results are consistent with previous evidence describing turmeric
and its bioactive compounds as potential modulators of systemic redox balance,
reducing lipid peroxidation and strengthening endogenous antioxidant defenses.
[13,21]. Considering that lipid peroxidation constitutes a central component of
oxidative stress, the reduction in TBARS levels may reflect a more favorable redox
status [14,22].
Curcumin, the main bioactive compound of turmeric, is widely described as a
modulator of oxidative stress, acting both through direct neutralization of ROS and
through the induction of endogenous antioxidant systems [11,12]. Therefore, the
reduction in lipid peroxidation markers and the increase in antioxidant capacity
observed in this study are b iologically plausible and suggest a potential adjuvant
role of curcumin in modulating oxidative disturbances associated with chronic HIV
infection, a hypothesis that should be confirmed in future studies [23,24].
An additional explanation for the limited cytokine response observed may relate
to the biological hierarchy of curcumin’s mechanisms of action. Curcumin primarily
modulates redox balance through activation of antioxidant pathways, such as Nrf2
signaling [1,12,25], which may resul t in earlier changes in oxidative stress
biomarkers compared to inflammatory cytokines. In contrast, markers such as IL -6
and TNF -α reflect complex immune regulatory processes influenced by chronic
immune activation, antiretroviral exposure, and host-related factors in people living

23

with HIV [2,4–6]. Therefore, redox improvements may precede detectable systemic
anti-inflammatory effects, especially in studies with short follow -up and limited
sample size [1,4,12].
Regarding lipid outcomes, a significant group × time interaction was observed
only for total cholesterol, with a reduction between M1 and M3 in the group that
started with placebo, while no significant changes were observed in the group that
started with curcumin. This finding reinforces the lack of evidence for a specific lipid
effect attributable to curcumin within this study design. The metabolic heterogeneity
of people living with HIV, prolonged exposure to antiretroviral therapy (ART), and
the reduced sample size may have limited the detection of lipid effects exclusively
attributable to curcumin.
This study has limitations, including the small sample size, which reduces
statistical power for comparisons between conditions; the inherent susceptibility of
crossover designs to residual and period effects; and potential time -related
confounding factors, such as lifestyle changes, regression to the mean, and the

participation in a clinical study and systematic follow -up. Additionally, the
discrepancy between the primary outcomes defined in the trial registry and the more

SUPLEMENTAÇÃO DE CURCUMINA E ALTERAÇÕES AO LONGO
DO TEMPO EM MARCADORES DE ESTRESSE METABÓLICO,
INFLAMATÓRIO E OXIDATIVO EM PESSOAS VIVENDO COM HIV
E DISLIPIDEMIA: UM ENSAIO CLÍNICO RANDOMIZADO, DUPLO-
CEGO E CRUZADO

Resumo
Pessoas vivendo com HIV (PVHIV) apresentam ativação imune persistente,
estresse oxidativo e alta prevalência de distúrbios metabólicos, incluindo
dislipidemia, que aumentam o risco cardiovascular. A curcumina, um composto
polifenólico derivado da Curcuma l onga, exibe propriedades antioxidantes e anti -
inflamatórias e pode representar uma estratégia adjuvante para a modulação redox
e metabólica. Este estudo avaliou os efeitos da suplementação com curcumina
sobre marcadores metabólicos, inflamatórios e de estr esse oxidativo em PVHIV
com dislipidemia. Um ensaio clínico cruzado, randomizado, duplo -cego e
controlado por placebo foi conduzido em um serviço especializado em atendimento
a pessoas vivendo com HIV no sul do Brasil. Adultos em terapia antirretroviral
estável por pelo menos seis meses e com diagnóstico de dislipidemia receberam
curcumina (1000 mg/dia) ou placebo durante dois períodos de intervenção
separados por uma fase de washout. Os desfechos bioquímicos incluíram perfil
lipídico, enzimas hepáticas, gl icose, citocinas inflamatórias (IL -6, IL-10, TNF-α) e
marcadores de estresse oxidativo [substâncias reativas ao ácido tiobarbitúrico
(TBARS) e capacidade antioxidante total (CAT)]. Os dados foram analisados por
meio de ANOVA de medidas repetidas, avalian do grupo, tempo e interação grupo
× tempo. Dezesseis participantes foram incluídos (idade média de 44,7 ± 1,2 anos;
68,8% do sexo feminino ), com adesão adequada. Uma interação grupo × tempo
significativa foi observada apenas para o colesterol total (p = 0,034). Efeitos
significativos do tempo foram identificados para o colesterol HDL (p = 0,004),
triglicerídeos (p = 0,003), AST (p = 0,021), hemoglobina glicada (p = 0,014), TBARS
plasmático (p = 0,049) e CAT (p = 0,003). Observou -se redução nos níveis de
triglicerídeos e TBARS, além de aumento na capacidade antioxidante, ao longo do
período de acompanhamento, independentemente da sequência de intervenção.
As citocinas inflamatórias apresentaram marcada variabilidade interindividual. A

suplementação com curcumina associou-se a alterações longitudinais no estresse
oxidativo e em marcadores metabólicos, embora os efeitos específicos do
tratamento em comparação com o placebo tenham sido limitados. Ensaios clínicos
de maior porte, com desfechos oxidativos predefinidos, são necessários para
confirmar esses achados.

CURCUMIN SUPPLEMENTATION AND CHANGES OVER TIME IN METABOLIC,
INFLAMMATORY, AND OXIDATIVE STRESS MARKERS IN PEOPLE LIVING WITH HIV
AND DYSLIPIDEMIA: A RANDOMIZED DOUBLE-BLIND CROSSOVER TRIAL

Abstract
People living with HIV (PLHIV) present persi stent immune activation, oxidative
stress, and a high prevalence of metabolic disturbances, including dyslipidemia,
which increase cardiovascular risk. Curcumin, a polyphenolic compound derived
from Curcuma longa, exhibits antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties and may
represent an adjuvant strategy for redox and metabolic modulation. This study
evaluated the effects of curcumin supplementation on metabolic, inflammatory, and
oxidative stress markers in PLHIV with dyslipidemia. A randomized, double -blind,
placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial was conducted at a specialized HIV care
service in southern Brazil. Adults receiving stable antiretroviral therapy for at least
six months and diagnosed with dyslipidemia received curcumin (1000 mg/day) or
placebo during two intervention periods separated by a washout phase. Biochemical
outcomes included lipid profile, liver enzymes, glucose, inflammatory cytokines (IL-
6, IL -10, TNF -α), and oxidative stress markers [thiobarbituric acid reactive
substances (TB ARS) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC)]. Data were analyzed
using repeated -measures ANOVA assessing group, time, and group × time
interaction. Sixteen participants were included (mean age 44.7 ± 1.2 years; 68.8%
female), with adequate adherence. A significant group × time interaction was
observed only for total cholesterol (p = 0.034). Significant time effects were identified
for HDL-cholesterol (p = 0.004), triglycerides (p = 0.003), AST (p = 0.021), glycated
hemoglobin (p = 0.014), plasma TBARS (p = 0.049), and TAC (p = 0.003).
Reductions in triglycerides and TBARS and increased antioxidant capacity were
observed throughout the follow -up, regardless of intervention sequence.
Inflammatory cytokines showed marked interindividual variability. Curcumin
supplementation was associated with longitudinal changes in oxidative stress and
metabolic markers, although treatment-specific effects versus placebo were limited.
Larger trials with predefined oxidative endpoints are needed to confirm these
findings.

Keywords: AIDS; Curcuma longa , Oxidative stress, Dyslipidemia, Inflammatory
markers

1. Introduction
Chronic HIV infection, even under sustained viral suppression with antiretroviral
therapy (ART), is characterized by persistent immune activation and systemic
oxidative stress. Viral proteins such as Tat, Nef, and gp120 contribute to increased
production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) through activation of NADPH oxidases
and mitochondrial dysfunction, while residual microbial translocation maintains
inflammatory signaling pathways, including NF -κB activation [1–4]. As a
consequence, people living with HIV (PLHIV) exhibit a persistent imbalance
between oxidant production and antioxidant defense mechanisms, even in the
absence of detectable viremia [4,5].
Dysregulation of redox homeostasis in treated HIV infection has been associated
with lipid peroxidation, endothelial dysfunction, metabolic alterations, and features
of accelerated aging [6,7]. Reduced glutathione availability, impaired activity of
antioxidant enzymes, and alterations in the Nrf2 –Keap1 pathway have been
described in this population, reinforcing the concept of HIV as a clinical model of
chronic immune activati on and sustained oxidative stress [5,8]. Although
antiretroviral therapy (ART) effectively controls viral replication, it does not fully
restore redox balance and may even contribute to mitochondrial dysfunction and
persistent oxidative damage [3,9]. This sustained pro -oxidant state is closely
associated with metabolic comorbidities frequently observed in people living with
HIV (PLHIV), including dyslipidemia and components of the metabolic syndrome
[7,10].
Curcumin, the main polyphenolic constituent of Curcuma longa L., has been
widely investigated for its pleiotropic biological properties. In addition to its direct
free-radical scavenging capacity, curcumin modulates key intracellular signaling
cascades, including inhibition of NF -κB activation, activation of the Nrf2 pathway,
regulation of mitochondrial function, and epigenetic modulation of inflammatory
gene expression [11,12]. Experimental studies demonstrate that curcumin
enhances endogenous antioxidant defenses through induction of heme oxygenase-
1 (HO-1) via Nrf2 activation and reduces lipid peroxidation and cytokine production
in inflammatory and metabolic models [13–15]. These findings suggest that

14

curcumin acts as a regulator of systemic redox homeostasis rather t han merely as
a conventional antioxidant.
Despite robust preclinical evidence supporting the redox -modulating properties
of curcumin, controlled clinical studies evaluating its mechanistic effects under
conditions characterized by persistent immune activation remain limited. In
particular, the pot ential of curcumin to modulate oxidative stress biomarkers in
treated HIV infection—a clinical context marked by chronic inflammatory signaling
and metabolic dysregulation—remains insufficiently explored [8,16].
Accordingly, the present randomized, double -blind, placebo -controlled
crossover clinical trial was designed to evaluate the effects of curcumin
supplementation on lipid profile (primary outcome) and, secondarily, to investigate
its influence on systemic biomarkers of oxidative stress and inflammation in people
living with HIV and dyslipidemia receiving stable antiretroviral therapy (ART), using
this population as a clinical model of chronic immune activation and redox
imbalance.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1 Study design
This study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical
trial conducted in accordance with the CONSORT guidelines and the principles of
the Declaration of Helsinki. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics
Committee of the State University of Western Paraná (protocol no. 7,049,856). All
participants provided written i nformed consent prior to inclusion. The trial was
registered in the Brazilian Clinical Trials Registry (ReBEC; RBR-7y5p3x8).

2.2 Study setting and participants
Participants were recruited from the Specialized Care Service (SAE/CTA) in
the municipality of Francisco Beltrão, Paraná, Brazil. Eligible individuals were adults
aged 35 to 50 years living with HIV, receiving stable antiretroviral therapy (ART) for
at least six months, and diagnosed with dyslipidemia according to the Brazilian
Guidelines for Dyslipidemia and Atherosclerosis Prevention [17]. Dyslipidemia was
defined as the presence of at least one abnormal lipid parameter: total cholesterol
≥190 mg/dL, HDL-cholesterol <40 mg/dL, or triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL.

15

Pregnant women and in dividuals unable to ingest capsules were excluded.
Participants were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time
without any impact on their routine clinical care.

Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to one of two intervention
sequences: curcumin followed by placebo or placebo followed by curcumin. The
randomization s equence was computer -generated in blocks by an independent
pharmacist who was not involved in data collection or statistical analysis. Allocation
concealment was ensured through the use of coded bottles. Participants,
researchers, laboratory staff, and sta tisticians remained blinded to treatment
allocation throughout the study. The assessments were carried out at four time
points (T1–T4), as shown in the table.

2.4 Intervention
The intervention consisted of the administration of 1000 mg/day of Curcuma
longa L. (rhizome) dry extract, standardized to 95% curcuminoids, provided as two
500 mg capsules. The botanical material was taxonomically identified by a qualified
botanist, and a voucher specimen was deposited in the Herbarium of Itaipu
Binacional under registration number 05.06/24. The plant material consisted of dried
rhizomes of Curcuma longa L.
The botanical material was obtained from certified suppliers and
manufactured according to Good Compounding Practices, in accordance with
ANVISA RDC No. 67/2007. T he extract (CUR240401) was standardized to 95%
curcuminoids, as determined in the analytical report validated by the manufacturer.
Each intervention period lasted 12 weeks and was separated by a 4 -week
washout period, based on pharmacokinetic consideratio ns related to curcumin
metabolism and elimination [18].
The placebo contained the same excipients, with the addition of food coloring,
ensuring similar sensory characteristics.

17

2.5 Sample size
The sample size calculation was performed using G*Power software,
considering α = 0.05, statistical power of 80%, and an effect size of 0.25, resulting
in a minimum estimated sample of 34 participants. Due to recruitment limitations,
the final sample consi sted of 16 participants, and this limitation was taken into
account in the interpretation of the results.

2.6 Laboratory analyses
Blood samples were collected after a minimum fasting period of 12 hours.
Routine biochemical analyses (total cholesterol, triglycerides, AST, ALT, and
fasting glucose) were performed using commercial kits (Ebram) in a semi-automatic
spectrophotometer (BT 3000 Plus). Glycated hemoglobin was determined using
Analisa® kits. Inflammatory cytokines (IL -6, IL-10, and TNF -α) were qu antified by
ELISA (Thermo Fisher Scientific), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Oxidative stress biomarkers were analyzed at the Laboratory of Human and Animal
BioHealth (Federal University of Fronteira Sul). Intracellular ROS production was
assessed using the DCHF -DA assay, as described by Loetchutinat et al. [19].
Fluorescence was measured with excitation at 488 nm and emission at 520 nm, and
results were expressed in arbitrary units (AU). TBARS, total antioxidant capacity
(TAC), total thiols, and vitamin C were determined using standardized
spectrophotometric methods.

2.7 Outcomes and Statistical Analysis
The primary outcome was the change in lipid profile (total cholesterol, HDL -
c, LDL -c, and triglycerides). Secondary outcomes included oxidative stress
biomarkers (TBARS, TAC, total thiols, vitamin C, and ROS), inflammatory cytokines
(IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α), and metabolic parameters (fasting glucose, HbA1c, AST,
and ALT).
For sample characterization, categorical variables were described as
absolute and relative frequencies, and continuous variables as mean and standard
deviation. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro –Wilk test,
homogeneity of variances by Levene’s test, and sphericity by Mauchly’s test. When

18

necessary, logarithmic transformations were performed to meet the assumptions of
parametric statistics.
Considering the crossover design, comparisons between groups over time
were conducted using repeated -measures Analysis of Variance (ANOVA),
evaluating group effects, time effects, and group × time interaction effects. Due to
the small sample size , formal tests to assess sequence or carryover effects were
not performed, and the results were interpreted with caution.
Additionally, intragroup analyses were conducted using the nonparametric
Friedman test, comparing the four assessment time points with in each sequence.
All analyses were performed using SPSS software, version 29.0, with a significance
level set at 5% (p < 0.05).

4. Discussion
In this randomized, double -blind, placebo-controlled crossover clinical trial,
curcumin supplementation was associated with time -related changes in oxidative
stress markers and some metabolic parameters in people living with HIV (PLWH)
with dyslipidemia. Although lipid parameters were defined as the primary outcomes
in the study registration, the most consistent longitudinal signals were observed in
redox biomarkers, with a reduction in plasma TBARS and an increase in antioxidant
capacity over the follow -up period. This pattern suggests that curcumin may exert
earlier or more readily detectable effects on redox balance than on lipid metabolism
in this clinical context.
Oxidative stress is recognized as a central component of HIV -1 infection, being
present from the early stages of the disease, increasing as the disease progresses,
and persisting even in individuals receiving effective antiretroviral therapy. Evidence
indicates that HIV infection promotes redox imbalance through the dysregulation of
multiple cellular pathways, resulting in increased ROS production and mitochondrial
dysfunction [9]. This increase in ROS is mediated by several viral proteins, including
the envelope glycoprotein gp120, Tat, Nef, Vpr, and reverse transcriptase, which
act complementarily across different cell types. The activation of pro -oxidant
systems, such as NADPH oxidases, cytochrome P450 2E1, and enzymes involved
in polyamine metabolism, contributes to excessive ROS generation, affecting
immune cells, cells of the central nervous system, and endothelial cells, thereby
reinforcing the systemic nature of oxidative st ress associated with HIV -1 infection
[4].
Oxidative stress is markedly exacerbated in people living with HIV com pared
with healthy controls, progressively increasing as the disease advances, with higher

22

levels observed in symptomatic compared with asymptomatic individuals. Evidence
indicates that although antiretroviral therapy (ART) is effective in suppressing vira l
replication, it is not sufficient to fully normalize redox balance and may even
contribute to the maintenance of oxidative stress through mitochondrial alterations,
residual inflammation, and metabolic effects associated with chronic antiretroviral
use [5]. This scenario favors the persistence of a pro -oxidant state associated with
metabolic disturbances, chronic inflammatory activation, immunosenescence, and
accelerated aging, even in individuals with undetectable viral load [3,20]
In this context, the findings of the present study gain biological rel evance. A
significant time effect was observed, with a reduction in plasma TBARS, a classical
marker of lipid peroxidation, and a progressive increase in total antioxidant capacity
assessed by the ferric reducing antioxidant power assay, regardless of trea tment
sequence. These results are consistent with previous evidence describing turmeric
and its bioactive compounds as potential modulators of systemic redox balance,
reducing lipid peroxidation and strengthening endogenous antioxidant defenses.
[13,21]. Considering that lipid peroxidation constitutes a central component of
oxidative stress, the reduction in TBARS levels may reflect a more favorable redox
status [14,22].
Curcumin, the main bioactive compound of turmeric, is widely described as a
modulator of oxidative stress, acting both through direct neutralization of ROS and
through the induction of endogenous antioxidant systems [11,12]. Therefore, the
reduction in lipid peroxidation markers and the increase in antioxidant capacity
observed in this study are b iologically plausible and suggest a potential adjuvant
role of curcumin in modulating oxidative disturbances associated with chronic HIV
infection, a hypothesis that should be confirmed in future studies [23,24].
An additional explanation for the limited cytokine response observed may relate
to the biological hierarchy of curcumin’s mechanisms of action. Curcumin primarily
modulates redox balance through activation of antioxidant pathways, such as Nrf2
signaling [1,12,25], which may resul t in earlier changes in oxidative stress
biomarkers compared to inflammatory cytokines. In contrast, markers such as IL -6
and TNF -α reflect complex immune regulatory processes influenced by chronic
immune activation, antiretroviral exposure, and host-related factors in people living

23

with HIV [2,4–6]. Therefore, redox improvements may precede detectable systemic
anti-inflammatory effects, especially in studies with short follow -up and limited
sample size [1,4,12].
Regarding lipid outcomes, a significant group × time interaction was observed
only for total cholesterol, with a reduction between M1 and M3 in the group that
started with placebo, while no significant changes were observed in the group that
started with curcumin. This finding reinforces the lack of evidence for a specific lipid
effect attributable to curcumin within this study design. The metabolic heterogeneity
of people living with HIV, prolonged exposure to antiretroviral therapy (ART), and
the reduced sample size may have limited the detection of lipid effects exclusively
attributable to curcumin.
This study has limitations, including the small sample size, which reduces
statistical power for comparisons between conditions; the inherent susceptibility of
crossover designs to residual and period effects; and potential time -related
confounding factors, such as lifestyle changes, regression to the mean, and the
potential Hawthorne effect, characterized by behavioral modifications resulting from
participation in a clinical study and systematic follow -up. Additionally, the
discrepancy between the primary outcomes defined in the trial registry and the more
consistent redox -related changes observed should be interpreted strictly as an
exploratory finding rather than evidence of primary efficacy. Despite these
limitations, the consistent direction of redox modulation observed supports the need
for further investigation s in larger, adequately powered trials with prespecified
oxidative stress outcomes and longer follow-up periods.
